d.title: Hit@K was one metric; the others need the whole relevant set
d.caption: Every measurement in module 5 asked a binary question: did *any* chunk in the top k come from the right document and contain the answer. That is Hit@K, and the five other standard metrics need **the full set of relevant chunks**, which has to be labelled. Building it changes the character of the golden set: across these twenty queries the relevant set runs from **1 chunk to 39**, with a median of 6 — so a single query's precision ceiling at k=5 varies from 0.20 to 1.00 before the retriever does anything.

d.title: The re-ranking claim: true on a weak first stage, false on a strong one
d.caption: The claim is falsifiable — a cross-encoder is supposed to move MRR and nDCG once the right chunk is already in the set. On the dense retriever it does, and more: **every metric improves**, with Hit@5 reaching 1.00. On RRF fusion, which was already at Hit@5 = 1.00, the same re-ranker **takes Hit@5 down to 0.90** and moves MRR and R@5 slightly backwards. So a cross-encoder is not a free improvement; it is a second opinion that can overrule a better first one.

d.title: Precision and recall move in opposite directions, so k is a choice of metric
d.caption: As k rises, Hit@k and R@k climb and **P@k collapses, 0.75 to 0.26**. nDCG@k is nearly flat across the whole range, which makes it the one number that does not simply restate your choice of k. The practical consequence: "optimise recall first" is good advice precisely because recall is the only one of these that cannot be bought by changing k, and the others can.

d.title: Two RAGAS scores restate the IR metrics; two see something new
d.caption: The metrics above grade **retrieval** and need no model, so they are free, deterministic and CI-able. RAGAS grades the **generation** on top, and its scores are LLM-judged — more expensive, non-deterministic, and measuring things no IR metric can reach. Which is the useful split: context precision and recall overlap with P@K and R@K and should probably be taken from those instead, and **faithfulness and answer relevancy have no cheaper substitute**.

d.title: The scale ladder correlates with memory, not latency
d.caption: The standard thresholds — under 100K, 100K to 10M, beyond — track something real, and 5.5 measured what. At **one million vectors flat search is 74.5 ms**, which is still small beside an LLM call; the number that has become a problem is **1,536 MB of RAM**. So the ladder's rungs are memory boundaries wearing latency's clothes, and the decisions they force — quantize, shard, move off-heap — are all about bytes.

d.title: Three update strategies, and when each is the only option
d.caption: The index clock and the query clock run separately, and this is the decision about how fast the slow one ticks. **Incremental by content hash is the right default** — 6.8 measures the hash check at 1.3 ms against a 13.2-second rebuild. A full rebuild is the only option when the embedding model changes, because 6.8's mismatch measurement shows mixed vectors silently halve recall. Event-driven has the lowest staleness and needs the source system to cooperate.

d.title: A rebuild in place is worse than stale — it is arbitrary
d.caption: A full rebuild has a failure mode incremental updates do not: **while it runs the index is partially populated**, so queries return whatever has been written so far. That is not stale data, which is at least consistent and explainable — it is an arbitrary subset, and a user who asks the same question twice during the rebuild gets two different answers for no reason they could discover. Build into a new index and swap an alias.

d.title: The production checklist, weighted by what this module measured
d.caption: Two items change rank once measured. **Re-ranking is conditional, not high** — 6.1 measured it helping a weak first stage and *hurting* a strong one, so it needs a before-and-after on your own set. And **evaluation is the highest-weight item** because nothing else on the list is decidable without it. The cheapest item is incremental indexing, at a 1.3 ms hash check.

d.title: Parsing, which sits before the highest-leverage decision
d.caption: 5.4 established chunking as the highest-leverage decision in the pipeline. Parsing sits **before** it with the same property and far less attention: **a table flattened into a column of orphaned numbers cannot be rescued by any chunk size, any embedding model or any re-ranker.** Two rows lose nothing if you are careful and the rest lose structure that was the meaning — and the last row loses *everything* if you skip it.

d.title: Standard RAG works on turn one and breaks on turn two
d.caption: Embedding the latest user message works until the message stops being self-contained — and **a follow-up usually is not, because the subject lives in the previous turn**. *"And what about the second one?"* embeds to nothing useful. The fix is a generation before the retrieval: rewrite the follow-up into a standalone question using the history, then retrieve on the rewrite. Same shape as HyDE, same cost: a full model call on the critical path.

nodes.label: A model call on the critical path

d.title: If a constraint is exactly expressible, it is a filter
d.caption: Stated as a rule: **this tenant, this year, this department, this access level — these should be filters, not hopes about cosine similarity.** An embedding has no notion of exactness, so a constraint expressed in the query text is a preference the retriever may ignore. And the ordering matters as much as the existence: 6.8 measures post-filtering returning 19 foreign rows at identical recall, because it searched everything and dropped afterwards.

nodes.label: Put it in the query text

d.title: Proof that multi-hop is structural, not a tuning problem
d.caption: Every improvement so far has been a dial — better chunking moved recall a few points, hybrid search took 95% to 100%, HyDE moved one query from rank 15 to rank 1. This is not a dial. The question *"What companies did the CEO of the acquirer of Instagram work for?"* needs four hops, and the check is simple: **does any chunk contain both endpoints?** Across all six chunks the answer is no, every time. There is no k, no re-ranker and no embedding model that retrieves a passage which does not exist.

steps.note: 0 of 6 - the answer is a path

d.title: Three question shapes with the same property
d.caption: They share it for one reason: **the answer is not written down in any passage.** A multi-hop answer is a path. An aggregation answer is a union over fifty documents. A relationship answer is an edge sequence, recorded only if somebody happened to write that particular sentence. A graph stores the edges explicitly, which is what makes the traversal possible at all — and the cost is an extraction step that has to get the entities right.

nodes.label: None is written in a passage

d.title: Community summaries give corpus-level questions something to retrieve
d.caption: GraphRAG's extra step answers the aggregation case: detect communities of related entities, **summarise each with a model**, and route broad questions to those summaries rather than to chunks. *"What are the main themes in this corpus?"* then has a target, which standard RAG never does. The cheap version — label propagation, where each node repeatedly adopts its neighbours' commonest label — **converged in 2 passes** and recovered the obvious structure: Apple and its people, Meta and its people, and Zuckerberg's pre-Facebook projects as a third group.

d.title: Seven scenarios, and two where the answer is neither
d.caption: GraphRAG is the answer for four of these and **overkill for three**. The two rows worth dwelling on are the ones where both options are wrong: aggregation over a table is exactly and cheaply answered by 5.12's text-to-SQL, and under about fifty documents **you should put all of it in the context** — retrieval is the wrong tool too, not merely the weaker one.
